standard.title: Exchange information in familiar contexts
standard.description: interact with others using modelled language to exchange information in familiar contexts about self and personal worlds
standard.prior_knowledge: No formal prior study of the target language assumed (Y7-10 Entry sequence). Students bring general communicative competence in English and may have informal or incidental exposure to the target language. They have not yet learned to operate within the conventions and structures of the target language to exchange personal information.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students interact with others in the target language using modelled language structures to exchange information about themselves, their families, routines and personal worlds in familiar contexts, making appropriate choices about formality.

nodes.label: Greetings and basic social exchanges
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can exchange greetings and basic social courtesies in the target language, choosing appropriate formal or informal register.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a small set of modelled greetings and leave-takings in at least one context (e.g. greeting a teacher or peer).
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish formal and informal greetings; use modelled phrases to greet, farewell and respond to social courtesies across classroom and simulated social contexts.
wider: Compare greeting conventions across two or more cultures where the target language is spoken — identify where register rules differ from English conventions
Explore how greeting conventions shift across digital communication contexts (messaging, email) vs spoken interaction in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Greeting and register conventions are the entry point to all subsequent interaction. Students who have not internalised the formal/informal distinction will misapply register throughout EC01 and EC02 — an error that compounds across all spoken interaction descriptors.

response_modes.reason: Students need repeated, low-stakes exposure to greetings across varied simulated contexts before register choices become automatic. Role-play, choral practice and modelled exchanges build the repertoire from which appropriate selection can occur.
Varying the social context (peer, teacher, stranger, digital) ensures register awareness does not lock to a single modelled example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Exploring greeting conventions across different cultural communities where the target language is spoken gives early, concrete entry into intercultural understanding — one of the central threads of the Languages curriculum.
success_criteria: Can produce at least two contextually appropriate greetings in the target language (one formal, one informal)
Can identify and correct a register mismatch when given a scenario (e.g. using informal language with a teacher)

nodes.label: Introducing and describing self and others
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can introduce themselves and others and describe personal details (name, age, family, possessions) using modelled structures in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Introduce themselves using at least three personal details (e.g. name, where they live, one family member) with modelled structures.
nodes.typical_width: Introduce and describe self, family members and peers; describe possessions and basic personal characteristics; respond to and ask simple questions about personal worlds using modelled language.
wider: Produce a short multimodal self-introduction (e.g. a short recorded or illustrated profile) combining spoken and written target language
Interview a peer and introduce them to the class — shifting from first person to third person structures
nodes.hinge_reason: First- and third-person structures used for self-description underpin the grammar nodes (EU02) and all subsequent personal exchange tasks. Students who cannot produce these with basic accuracy will be unable to participate meaningfully in EC01's interview and conversation tasks.

response_modes.reason: Accuracy in person agreement and possessive structures requires practice to become reliable. Errors here (e.g. person agreement, possessives) are procedural rather than conceptual — massed practice with corrective feedback is the lever.

success_criteria: Can introduce themselves using at least three accurate modelled structures covering name, location and family
Can respond accurately to simple personal questions from a peer or teacher in the target language

nodes.label: Expressing likes, dislikes and preferences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express likes, dislikes and preferences about familiar topics using modelled structures in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Express at least one like and one dislike using a modelled structure tied to a familiar topic (e.g. hobbies, food).
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of modelled structures to express and compare likes, dislikes and preferences across multiple familiar topics; respond to others' expressions of preference with simple agreement or contrast.
wider: Survey peers about their preferences and compile results — shifting from personal to aggregated expression ('most people in our class like…')
Compare how preference is expressed differently across formal and informal registers in the target language

response_modes.reason: Students need to encounter preference expression across enough topic areas (hobbies, food, music, sport) that they can transfer the structure flexibly rather than being locked to one rehearsed topic.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Expressing preferences is the structural foundation for opinion exchange in EC02 and discussion in Y9-10. Varied topic contexts now build transfer that pays dividends across the full secondary languages sequence.
success_criteria: Can express at least one like and one dislike using a modelled structure in the target language
Can respond to a peer's expressed preference with a simple agreement or contrast

nodes.label: Exchanging information about routines and daily life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can interact with others to exchange information about routines, events and daily life activities using modelled language in familiar contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Participate in a structured exchange (question and answer format) about at least one aspect of daily routine using modelled language.
nodes.typical_width: Conduct and respond to simple interviews or conversations about routines, leisure activities, significant events and daily life; use modelled language associated with time and place to add context to exchanges.
wider: Interact (via secure digital platforms where available) with peers or simulated peers from a target language community — comparing daily routines across cultural contexts
Extend exchanges to include past or future events using emerging tense structures, connecting to EU02

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the greetings, self-description and preference structures from nodes 1–3 into sustained, contextualised interaction. Teaching investment is in supporting students to move fluidly across structures within a single exchange rather than producing each in isolation.

success_criteria: Can ask and respond to at least three questions about daily routines in a structured exchange in the target language
Uses modelled time or place language to contextualise at least one statement in the exchange
